trial_name: VIOLET — Early High-Dose Vitamin D3 for Critically Ill, Vitamin D–Deficient Patients (2019)
citation: National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute PETAL Clinical Trials Network; Ginde AA, Brower RG, Caterino JM, Finck L, Banner-Goodspeed VM, Grissom CK, et al. Early high-dose vitamin D3 for critically ill, vitamin D-deficient patients. N Engl J Med. 2019 Dec 26;381(26):2529-2540.
evidence_level: High-quality RCT (early stopping for futility reduces precision)
one_liner: Single enteral 540,000 IU vitamin D3 bolus given early to vitamin D-deficient ICU patients did not reduce 90-day mortality compared with placebo (23.5% vs 20.6%, P=0.26).

pico.population: Adults with an ICU admission decision and point-of-care 25-hydroxyvitamin D <20 ng/mL, within 12 hours of ICU decision, with a qualifying acute condition (e.g., pneumonia, sepsis, shock, mechanical ventilation for acute respiratory failure).
pico.intervention: Single enteral dose of cholecalciferol 540,000 IU (liquid), administered orally or via nasogastric/orogastric tube within 2 hours of randomization; clinicians asked to avoid additional vitamin D testing or supplementation for 1 month.
pico.comparison: Matched placebo, same volume and route, administered within the same time window.
pico.outcome: All-cause mortality at 90 days (primary); also 28-day mortality, in-hospital mortality, patient-centred recovery endpoint, ventilator-free days, safety (hypercalcaemia, kidney stones).

background.existing_knowledge: Vitamin D deficiency is common in critically ill adults; observational studies link low 25-hydroxyvitamin D to infection, lung injury, organ dysfunction, and mortality. Prior RCT, VITdAL-ICU, did not shorten hospital length of stay overall but suggested possible benefit in severe deficiency subgroup.
background.knowledge_gap: Whether a single high-dose enteral vitamin D3 bolus given very early in critical illness improves survival or recovery in vitamin D-deficient patients.
background.hypothesis: Early high-dose vitamin D3 reduces 90-day all-cause mortality in vitamin D-deficient ICU patients.

methods.design: Randomised, multicentre, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial within the NHLBI PETAL Clinical Trials Network (United States).
methods.setting: Multicentre, PETAL network sites in the United States; enrolment from emergency department, hospital ward, operating theatre, or transfer hospitals.

inclusion: Adults with an ICU admission decision
At least one qualifying acute condition (pneumonia, sepsis, shock, mechanical ventilation for acute respiratory failure, aspiration, smoke inhalation, pancreatitis, lung contusion)

methods.intervention: Single enteral dose of cholecalciferol 540,000 IU (liquid), given orally or via nasogastric/orogastric tube within 2 hours of randomisation. No mandated co-interventions; clinicians were asked to avoid additional vitamin D testing or supplementation for 1 month.
methods.comparison: Matched placebo, single enteral dose, identical administration window and route.
methods.blinding: Double-blind (participants, clinicians, investigators, outcome assessors); central electronic allocation with concealment.
methods.sample_size_power: Planned enrolment of 3000 to detect a 5% absolute mortality reduction (20% to 15%) with 87% power at two-sided α=0.05, with 3 interim analyses and a Bayesian futility rule. Early termination for futility after 1360 randomised.
methods.primary_outcome: All-cause mortality at 90 days in the prespecified confirmed-deficiency population.
secondary_outcomes: Alive and at home under previous level of care at day 90 (patient-centred recovery)
methods.follow_up: 90 days after randomisation; additional assessments at 28 days and day 7 for selected physiological endpoints.

headline_bullets: Early bolus vitamin D3 did not reduce 90-day mortality (23.5% vs 20.6%; P=0.26) despite strong biochemical separation (day-3 25-hydroxyvitamin D 46.9 vs 11.4 ng/mL).
Key secondary outcomes showed no improvement; point estimates often numerically favoured placebo (e.g., 28-day mortality 17.3% vs 13.1%; risk difference 4.3%, 95% CI -0.1 to 8.6).
Clinically important harms were not apparent: hypercalcaemia 2.7% vs 2.1% (P=0.51), kidney stones 0.0% vs 0.6% (P=0.25).

outcomes_table.outcome: Death from any cause to day 90 (primary, confirmed deficiency)
outcomes_table.note: Primary endpoint; denominators exclude those lost to follow-up for day-90 status.

outcomes_table.outcome: Death from any cause to day 28 (confirmed deficiency)
Death in hospital to day 90 (confirmed deficiency)
Alive and at home under previous level of care at day 90 (confirmed deficiency)

outcomes_table.note: Higher is better; no signal of benefit.

outcomes_table.outcome: Death from any cause to day 90 (screened-deficient population, point-of-care positive)
outcomes_table.note: Prespecified broader analysis, consistent with primary.

safety: Hypercalcaemia to day 14: 2.7% (vitamin D3) vs 2.1% (placebo), P=0.51.
Kidney stones to day 90: 0.0% vs 0.6%, P=0.25.
No other major safety signals were detected.

domains.notes: Central electronic randomisation with permuted blocks stratified by site; double-blind design ensures concealment.
Double-blind; primary outcome (all-cause mortality) is objective.

2 randomised participants excluded (inadequate consent, withdrawal); day-90 vital status missing for 7 vs 12 in primary analysis (low, balanced). Primary analysis on confirmed-deficiency subset is not pure ITT.
Study drug administered in 532/538 (98.9%) vs 532/540 (98.5%); wrong-drug rare (1 vs 3).
Well balanced; mean age ~55 years, SOFA ~5.5, baseline 25-hydroxyvitamin D ~11 ng/mL.
Prespecified Bayesian futility thresholds; early stopping reduces precision and ability to exclude small effects.
Day-3 25-hydroxyvitamin D 46.9 vs 11.4 ng/mL (MD 35.5) confirms strong biochemical effect.

internal_validity.verdict: Moderate. Randomisation, blinding, objective primary outcome, and strong biochemical separation support causal inference, but early stopping for futility reduced power/precision and the prespecified confirmed-deficiency primary analysis population departs from a pure ‘all randomised’ ITT framework.

domains.notes: Broad inclusion of common ICU syndromes (pneumonia, sepsis, shock, ARF); required rapid consent/surrogate and enteral access. Excluded patients unable to take enteral medications, with hypercalcaemia, kidney stone history, or imminent death.

Most applicable to high-resource ICUs able to perform rapid point-of-care screening and early enteral bolus. Generalisability limited for severe malnutrition, delayed ICU access, or different vitamin D status distributions.

external_validity.verdict: Generalisability is reasonable for early ICU admissions in similar high-resource hospitals, but extrapolation to patients without enteral access, with contraindications to high-dose vitamin D, or with extreme deficiency/longer-duration critical illness is limited.

strengths: Pragmatic ‘screen early, treat early’ design aligned with real-world implementation.
Double-blind randomised methodology with objective primary outcome.
Strong physiological separation in measured 25-hydroxyvitamin D concentrations by day 3.
Low loss to follow-up for vital status to day 90.
limitations: Stopped early for futility, reducing power and narrowing inference to larger effect sizes.
Primary analysis population required confirmation of deficiency by reference assay after randomisation (departs from strict ITT).
Single bolus strategy does not test sustained supplementation during recovery.
Outcome table reporting emphasised P value for the primary endpoint without an accompanying effect estimate/CI in the main table.

critical_appraisal.summary: Despite a strong biochemical effect, a single early high-dose vitamin D3 bolus produced no clinical benefit in a well-conducted RCT; early stopping for futility limits precision but the trial provides robust evidence against a large mortality reduction.
strengths: Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled with concealed allocation.
Objective primary endpoint and low loss to follow-up.
Effective delivery confirmed by large increase in 25-hydroxyvitamin D.
weaknesses: Early termination reduces power; unable to exclude small effect sizes.
Primary analysis on confirmed-deficiency subset, not all-randomised ITT.
Single bolus design may not reflect benefits of sustained repletion.

sections.authors_conclusion: Routine early high-dose (540,000 IU) bolus vitamin D3 for critically ill patients selected by point-of-care low 25-hydroxyvitamin D is not supported.

clinical_bottom_line.verdict: Do not routinely administer high-dose bolus vitamin D3 to vitamin D-deficient ICU patients; no survival or recovery benefit was found.
clinical_bottom_line.applies_to: Adults with early critical illness and vitamin D deficiency (<20 ng/mL) who can take enteral medications.
clinical_bottom_line.does_not_mean: This does not imply that nutritional vitamin D repletion or sustained supplementation in severe, prolonged deficiency has no role.
implementation_caveats: Single bolus strategy tested; sustained or repeated dosing may have different effects.
Excluded patients unable to take enteral drugs or with hypercalcaemia/kidney stone history.
No evidence of harm, but also no evidence of benefit—de-implementation of indiscriminate testing and acute bolus supplementation is supported.

controversies.notes: Patients may have been too heterogeneous; benefit might be restricted to severe deficiency or specific inflammatory phenotypes.
Total 25-hydroxyvitamin D behaves as a negative acute-phase reactant, complicating eligibility targeting and mechanistic interpretation.
The single bolus rapidly corrected measured 25-hydroxyvitamin D but may not replicate potential benefits of sustained repletion; ongoing trials (VITDALIZE) address this.
VITdAL-ICU did not show overall benefit but had a possible signal in severe deficiency, motivating VIOLET.
Post-VIOLET meta-analyses have not demonstrated consistent mortality benefit from vitamin D supplementation in critical illness.
The VITDALIZE programme is evaluating high-dose vitamin D3 in critically ill adults with severe deficiency.
Paediatric Surviving Sepsis guidelines suggest against acute repletion in sepsis/septic shock; ESPEN emphasises cautious, targeted vitamin D use during nutritional support.

context_related_trials.relation: Earlier RCT that did not shorten hospital LOS overall but suggested possible mortality benefit in severe deficiency, motivating this larger definitive trial.
Ongoing phase III RCT (high-dose vitamin D3 in severe deficiency) that addresses targeting and regimen questions left open by VIOLET’s single-bolus design.

unresolved_questions: Does a sustained repletion strategy improve outcomes in patients with severe vitamin D deficiency?
Are there specific subphenotypes (e.g., ARDS, sepsis, severe deficiency) that could benefit from high-dose vitamin D?
What is the biological relevance of total 25-hydroxyvitamin D during acute inflammation, and should alternative biomarkers guide therapy?

numbers_to_remember: n=1360 randomized; primary analysis in 1078 with confirmed deficiency
28-day mortality: 17.3% vs 13.1%, risk difference 4.3% (95% CI -0.1 to 8.6)
quick_recall.one_line_takeaway: Early high-dose vitamin D3 bolus does not improve survival or recovery in vitamin D-deficient ICU patients; avoid routine screening and bolus supplementation in acute critical illness.
